q: You are planning anaesthesia for extraction of long-standing ICD leads. What is the most common major complication you must prepare for?
o: SVC injury with haemorrhage or tamponade
why: Major complications occur in 2–4%, usually SVC injury. Prepare a hybrid theatre, surgical bailout plan, cell salvage, arterial line, CVC, TOE, defib pads and femoral access for emergency bypass.

q: What is the most common indication for transvenous lead extraction?
why: More than half of extractions are for infection; these need prolonged antibiotics and delayed reimplantation.

q: A patient has had AF for 5 days and is not anticoagulated. Elective DC cardioversion is planned. What is needed first?
o: TOE to exclude left atrial thrombus
why: After more than 48 hours of AF there is a risk of atrial thrombus, which must be excluded on TOE (or by adequate anticoagulation) before cardioversion.

q: Using the modified Duke criteria, which combination makes a definite diagnosis of infective endocarditis?
why: Definite IE needs 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. Major: positive blood cultures or echo evidence.

q: A patient with mitral valve endocarditis has a 12 mm vegetation and has just had a splenic embolus. What is the best management?
why: Surgery is indicated with an embolic event and a vegetation over 10 mm, a vegetation over 15 mm, or ongoing severe valve dysfunction. Antibiotics run for 4–6 weeks with MDT input.

q: A 74-year-old in recovery has AF at 180/min with SBP 70 mmHg. Synchronised DC shocks are planned under sedation. What should happen to the oxygen at the moment of the shock?
o: Remove it just before the shock
Keep it on a non-rebreathe mask
why: Remove oxygen just before the shock (fire risk), then reapply. Apply pads before sedation, use up to three 80–200 J biphasic shocks, then amiodarone 300 mg IV if unsuccessful.

q: A patient with Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome needs anaesthesia for cardioversion. Which agent is best avoided?
why: In WPW avoid sympathetic stimulation (ketamine), anticholinergics and neostigmine, which can increase conduction down the accessory pathway.

q: Where is the ablation line placed for typical atrial flutter?
o: Between the IVC and the tricuspid valve
Across the slow AV nodal pathway
In the right ventricular outflow tract
why: Typical flutter is a right atrial circuit through the cavotricuspid isthmus (between IVC and TV). AF ablation isolates the pulmonary veins in the left atrium; AVNRT ablation targets the slow pathway.

q: Which is the main reason GA may be preferred to sedation for AF ablation?
o: It reduces the risk of tamponade
It is needed to induce the arrhythmia
Long procedures, less patient movement and easier TOE
It removes the need for heparin
why: GA suits prolonged procedures, reduces movement, aids TOE and may be the patient’s preference. Avoid suppressing arrhythmias when mapping inducible SVT/AVNRT.

q: Which tool estimates stroke risk to guide anticoagulation in AF?
why: CHA2DS2-VASc estimates stroke risk; HAS-BLED and ORBIT assess bleeding risk. Left atrial appendage closure is an option if anticoagulation is not possible.
